top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Given clinical and methodological heterogeneity across designs, settings, and outcomes, we conducted a narrative synthesis. Where available, we report effect measures with 95% CIs and p-values. We did not perform formal small-study or publication-bias tests because no meta-analysis was undertaken; instead, we qualitatively appraised potential reporting/publication biases and reflected these concerns within GRADE. Results from secondary research (systematic reviews) were used for context only and were not recombined with primary studies to avoid double counting.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.section: Methods > Study Design And Reporting Framework
top_evidence.text: This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [24]. In accordance with PRISMA, we prepared outcome-specific Summary of Findings tables (SoF) that collate study-level results per outcome and are provided as Additional Tables S1-S7. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; ID 897ub; 15 August 2024, available at h t t p s : / / o s f . i o/ 8 9 7 u b / ) [25]. The completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is available in Additional file 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Evidence suggests DA reduces GP workload and resource use (medications, imaging) while showing clinical outcomes similar to GP-referred pathways and no consistent signal of increased harms. Economic analyses from observational studies indicated neutral to moderate cost savings, though reliance on non-randomised data limits certainty.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Outcome-level certainty was graded with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE): risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, publication bias, indirectness [30]; Given the narrative synthesis without pooled estimates and the heterogeneity of outcomes precluding outcome-level aggregation, GRADE judgements were applied at the study level as inputs to the overall synthesis, consistent with guidance for reviews without meta-analysis. Economic evaluations published separately inherited the parent RCT's certainty rating. Dual independent grading (MaF and EB) with consensus.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Data were extracted using a standardised form adapted from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 6.3) [27], with pre-specified units/ scales (e.g., VAS 0-10 or 0-100, ODI 0-100, MSK-HQ 0-56, EQ-5D index) recorded as reported. Extracted items included authors, year, country, design, sample, intervention/comparator, outcomes, measurement tools, sources of funding, declared conflicts of interest, and key quantitative results. Participants were counted once per unique study or cohort to avoid double counting when the same cohort was reported across linked publications (e.g., primary study and linked economic evaluation) or contributed data to multiple outcomes. For transparency, all study-level quantitative results used to populate the SoF are reproduced verbatim in Additional Tables S1-S7, with units and time windows preserved. Two reviewers (MaF and EB) independently extracted data and reconciled discrepancies by consensus.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Across 14 studies, DA showed clinical outcomes similar to GP-referred care for pain, function (Musculoskeletal Health Questionnaire [MSK-HQ], Oswestry Disability Index [ODI]), and quality of life (EuroQol 5-Dimension [EQ-5D], 12-Item Short Form Health Survey [SF-12]) [36, 40, 41, 44]. Some RCTs suggested modest early benefits (e.g., -2.2 visual analogue scale [VAS] points at 6 weeks) [41], with no sustained differences mid-term [40, 41, 48]; where available, mean differences with 95% CIs are reported. Study-level clinical results (scales, timepoints, mean differences with 95% CI/p when available) are presented in Additional file 7 in Table S4 (SoF-Clinical outcomes).

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.section: Interpreting Certainty Of Evidence For Policy Decisions
top_evidence.text: The predominance of low and very low GRADE certainty ratings across outcomes reflects the observational nature of most included studies, a limitation inherent to health services research where randomization is often unfeasible or ethically problematic. This "low certainty" rating should not be interpreted as "poor quality evidence" but rather as appropriate epistemic humility given the study designs available. Importantly, low certainty does not imply that policy action should be deferred. GRADE guidance explicitly acknowledges that strong recommendations can be made despite low certainty evidence when: (i) the direction of effect is consistent across studies; (ii) the magnitude of potential benefits substantially outweighs potential harms; and (iii) the consequences of inaction The two studies achieving moderate certainty for selected outcomes (GP workload proxies, costs) provide an anchor of higher-confidence evidence, while the convergent findings from multiple lower-certainty studies across diverse healthcare systems provide corroborating support. For decision-makers, this triangulation of consistent findings offers a robust directional signal for policy, even if precise effect magnitudes remain uncertain. Future pragmatic trials and well-designed prospective cohorts could strengthen certainty, but should not be prerequisites for cautious implementation with appropriate monitoring.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.section: Risk Of Bias And Methodological Quality
top_evidence.text: Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed with Risk of Bias 2.0 (ROB 2.0) for RCTs [28] and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for observational studies [29]. Ratings were harmonized (low/moderate/high). Risk of bias assessments were performed independently by two reviewers (MaF and EB) with consensus resolution. Detailed study-level quality appraisals are summarized in Additional file 4. A cross-study bias matrix (randomization, selection, performance, detection, attrition, reporting, publication, language, setting, and confounding) is provided in Additional file 5.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: The combined searches identified 7,264 records (7,239 from databases and 25 from trial registries). After removal of duplicates, 5,003 unique records were screened. The initial search (15 July-15 October 2024) contributed 6,811 records; the updated search (1 January 2024-4 November 2025) yielded 453 additional records but no further eligible primary studies, likely reflecting evidence base stabilization and publication lag. After screening and eligibility assessment, 21 studies were included. The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram of study selection is presented in Fig. 1. The final sample comprised 7 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and 14 observational studies. Two economic evaluations published separately were linked to their respective parent RCTs for all quality and certainty assessments to avoid double counting.
